Mṛtyu-mukha literally means 'death's mouth' — death is imagined as a great beast with open jaws, ready to devour. All beings are already inside those jaws — birth places you in death's mouth. The question is not whether death will come but whether you can escape before the jaws close. The verse says that knowing the Self — the soundless, touchless, formless, imperishable reality — is the way out. The image is especially powerful because the speaker is Yama, Death himself. He is essentially saying: 'Here is how to escape from ME.' The Lord of Death is teaching the way to transcend death — the highest irony and the greatest compassion. The image also appears in Indian art — the Kīrtimukha (face of glory) and the Kāla-mukha (face of time/death) are fearsome faces with open mouths, representing the devouring power of time.

sk: नाचिकेतमुपाख्यानं मृत्युप्रोक्तं सनातनम् | उक्त्वा श्रुत्वा च मेधावी ब्रह्मलोके महीयते ||
ro: nāciketam · upākhyānaṁ · mṛtyuproktaṁ · sanātanam | uktvā · śrutvā · ca · medhāvī · brahmaloke · mahīyate ||
hi: मृत्यु (यम) द्वारा कहे गये इस सनातन नाचिकेत-उपाख्यान (कथा) को कहकर और सुनकर, मेधावी (बुद्धिमान्) पुरुष ब्रह्मलोक में महिमान्वित होता है।
en: Having recited and having heard this ancient tale of Nachiketa, told by Death — the wise one is glorified in the world of Brahman.

ws.e: tale, narrative — upa+ākhyāna; a subsidiary story with deep teaching
told by Death — mṛtyu (Death/Yama) + prokta (spoken); the authority of the teacher
eternal, ancient — this teaching is not new but timeless
having recited — absolutive of √vac; sharing the teaching
having heard — absolutive of √śru; receiving the teaching
the wise, the intelligent — one with medhā (wisdom, retentive power)

gr: mṛtyuproktam — 'spoken by Death': the authority claim is absolute — no higher authority on death exists than Death himself. sanātanam — 'eternal': the teaching is not a new invention but a timeless truth. uktvā śrutvā — 'having told and having heard': both the teacher and the student benefit — this is a reciprocal process. brahmaloke mahīyate — 'is glorified in Brahman's world': identical to 1.2.17.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.3.16 — A phala-śruti (statement of fruit/benefit) that encourages both the teaching and hearing of this text. The emphasis on 'mṛtyuprokta' (spoken by Death) underscores the unique authority of the Katha Upanishad — its teacher is Death himself.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि यह फल-श्रुति है — इस उपनिषद् का अध्ययन और शिक्षण दोनों मुक्तिदायक हैं। 'ब्रह्मलोक' = ब्रह्म-साक्षात्कार, कोई लोक नहीं।
advaita.en: Shankara says this is a phala-śruti — both studying and teaching this Upanishad are liberating. 'Brahmaloka' = Brahman-realisation, not a separate world.
advaita.ins: The act of sharing sacred knowledge is itself a spiritual practice — the teacher is transformed by teaching, the student by hearing.

vishisht.h: रामानुज 'उक्त्वा श्रुत्वा' में भागवत-सत्संग (divine fellowship) का महत्त्व देखते हैं — भगवत्-कथा कहना और सुनना दोनों भक्ति हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja sees in 'uktvā śrutvā' the importance of bhāgavata-satsaṅga (divine fellowship) — both telling and hearing divine stories are forms of devotion.
vishisht.ins: Sacred knowledge is meant to be shared — it grows by being given, not diminished.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं कि 'सनातनम्' (eternal) शब्द इस कथा की कालातीत प्रासंगिकता दर्शाता है — यह किसी एक युग की नहीं, सम्पूर्ण मानवता की कथा है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'sanātanam' (eternal) indicates the timeless relevance of this tale — it is not the story of one age but of all humanity.
aurobindo.ins: The dialogue between the soul and Death is not a historical event — it is the eternal conversation happening within every human being who dares to ask the ultimate question.

dp.q: 🔍 What is a 'phala-śruti' and why does the Upanishad include one?
dp.a: A phala-śruti ('statement of fruit') is a concluding passage that describes the benefits of studying, reciting, or meditating upon a particular text. It appears at the end of many Upanishads, hymns, and sacred texts. This verse is the phala-śruti for the first Adhyāya (chapters 1-3) of the Katha Upanishad. Its purpose is threefold: (1) Motivation: encouraging students to engage with the text by promising concrete spiritual benefits ('glorified in Brahman's world'). (2) Transmission: encouraging teachers to share the text ('uktvā' — having told) and students to seek it out ('śrutvā' — having heard), ensuring the teaching is passed on. (3) Authorization: the phrase 'mṛtyuproktam' (spoken by Death) reminds the reader/listener of the text's extraordinary source — this is not human speculation but Death's own testimony about what lies beyond death.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does the verse mention both 'telling' and 'hearing'?
dp.a: The phrase 'uktvā śrutvā ca' ('having told AND having heard') emphasises that the teaching-learning process is bilateral — both the teacher and the student are transformed. This is a fundamental principle of the guru-śiṣya tradition: the guru does not merely deposit information into a passive student; the act of teaching itself is a spiritual practice for the guru. When a teacher articulates the deepest truths, they re-discover those truths in the act of articulation. The student, by truly hearing (not just auditorily but with full attention and receptivity), opens themselves to the truth. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upanishad (2.4.5) uses the triple formula: 'ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ' — 'the Self is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon.' Hearing (śravaṇa) is the first step — but it must be a hearing so deep that it transforms the hearer.

sk: य इमं परमं गुह्यं श्रावयेद्ब्रह्मसंसदि | प्रयतः श्राद्धकाले वा तदानन्त्याय कल्पते तदानन्त्याय कल्पते ||
ro: ya · imaṁ · paramaṁ · guhyaṁ · śrāvayed · brahmasaṁsadi | prayataḥ · śrāddhakāle · vā · tad · ānantyāya · kalpate · tad · ānantyāya · kalpate ||
hi: जो इस परम गोपनीय (ज्ञान) को ब्रह्मसभा (विद्वत्सभा) में या श्राद्ध के अवसर पर पवित्र भाव से सुनाता है — वह अनन्त (फल) का अधिकारी होता है, अनन्त (फल) का अधिकारी होता है।
en: One who recites this supreme secret in a gathering of the wise, or at the time of the śrāddha ceremony, with due reverence — that qualifies one for the infinite, qualifies for the infinite.

ws.e: the supreme secret — parama (supreme) + guhya (secret, hidden)
in an assembly of Brahman-knowers — brahma (Brahman) + saṁsad (assembly)
with due reverence, with purity — pra+yata; having prepared oneself properly
at the time of śrāddha — the ceremony honouring ancestors; a sacred occasion

ws.h: अनन्तता (अनन्त फल) का अधिकारी होता है
ws.e: qualifies for the infinite — ānantya (infinity, endlessness) + kalpate (is fit for, qualifies)

gr: paramaṁ guhyam — 'supreme secret': the teaching is guhya (secret) not because it is withheld but because it is too subtle for casual comprehension. brahmasaṁsadi — 'in an assembly of Brahman-knowers': the teaching should be shared with the qualified, not broadcast indiscriminately. ānantyāya kalpate — 'qualifies for the infinite': repeated twice for emphasis. The duplication is the text's way of stamping 'CERTAIN' on the promise.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.3.17 — The concluding verse of the first Adhyāya. The repetition of 'tad ānantyāya kalpate' is a textual seal of emphasis. The verse specifies two contexts for sharing: brahmasaṁsad (assembly of wise) and śrāddhakāla (ancestor ceremony), indicating both philosophical and ritual settings.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'आनन्त्य' = मोक्ष, जो अनन्त (endless) है — कभी समाप्त नहीं होता। इस ज्ञान को योग्य श्रोताओं (ब्रह्मसंसद) में सुनाना स्वयं मोक्ष का साधन है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'ānantya' = mokṣa, which is infinite (endless) — it never ends. Reciting this knowledge to qualified listeners (brahmasaṁsad) is itself a means to mokṣa.
advaita.ins: Sharing true knowledge with the worthy is not merely generosity — it is a spiritual practice that liberates the teacher as much as the student.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि 'आनन्त्य' = भगवान् का शाश्वत सान्निध्य, जो अनन्त है। भगवत्-कथा को 'प्रयतः' (श्रद्धापूर्वक) सुनाने से अनन्त फल मिलता है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'ānantya' = the Lord's eternal presence, which is infinite. Reciting the Lord's story with reverence (prayataḥ) yields infinite fruit.
vishisht.ins: The repetition 'ānantyāya kalpate, ānantyāya kalpate' is the Upanishad's emphatic promise — the fruit of this knowledge is truly without end.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द 'आनन्त्य' (infinity) को चेतना की अनन्त विस्तार-अवस्था मानते हैं — परिमित चेतना से अपरिमित चेतना में संक्रमण। यही मानव विकास का लक्ष्य है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo reads 'ānantya' (infinity) as the state of infinite expansion of consciousness — the transition from finite to infinite consciousness. This is the goal of human evolution.
aurobindo.ins: The promise of the Upanishad is not a heavenly reward but an infinite expansion — becoming what you have always been but never fully realised.

dp.q: 🔍 Why is the promise repeated twice ('tad ānantyāya kalpate, tad ānantyāya kalpate')?
dp.a: The repetition of 'tad ānantyāya kalpate' (qualifies for the infinite) is a deliberate textual device found in Vedic and Upanishadic literature. Repetition at the end of a section serves as a textual seal — the equivalent of a signature stamp on a document. It conveys: (1) Certainty: 'I am not exaggerating; this is absolutely true.' (2) Emphasis: 'This is so important that I say it twice — do not overlook it.' (3) Structural closure: the repetition marks the end of the first Adhyāya (three Vallis). It tells the reciter and the listener: 'This section is complete.' In some traditions, the repetition is also connected to meditation practice: the phrase is meant to be dwelt upon, not just heard. Hearing it twice creates a deeper impression in consciousness — like a bell struck twice, the resonance lasts longer.

dp.q: 🔍 What does the closing of Adhyaya 1 signify for the Katha Upanishad's structure?
dp.a: The Katha Upanishad is divided into two Adhyāyas (chapters) of three Vallis (sections) each. Adhyāya 1 (Vallis 1-3) has now concluded. Its arc: Valli 1 — the story: Nachiketa goes to Death, waits three nights, receives three boons, asks the ultimate question ('What happens after death?'). Valli 2 — the ethics and epistemology: śreyas vs. preyas, vidyā vs. avidyā, OM as Brahman, the Self's immortality, the Self chooses whom it reveals itself to. Valli 3 — the psychology and practice: the chariot metaphor (Self/body/intellect/mind/senses), the hierarchy of being (senses → Purusha), the meditation technique (progressive absorption), the razor's edge, and the negative definition of the Self. Adhyāya 2 (Vallis 4-6) will deepen and complete the teaching: the city of eleven gates, the cosmic Person, the yoga of the Self, and Nachiketa's final liberation. The first Adhyāya has laid the foundation — the second will build the temple.
